Beginner foundation

What a MOSFET does in a circuit

A MOSFET is a voltage-controlled device. The gate voltage controls how easily current can flow between drain and source, while the insulated gate ideally draws essentially no steady current.

Control terminal

The gate electric field creates or removes mobile charge under the oxide. Ideally, \(i_G=0\).

Current path

When a channel exists, drain current flows through the channel between drain and source.

Body terminal

The body forms pn junctions with source and drain and influences threshold voltage.

How this module connects to earlier topics

Module 2 introduced doped silicon, depletion regions, and pn junctions. The MOSFET uses two pn junctions to isolate source and drain from the body, plus a metal-oxide-semiconductor capacitor to control the surface carrier population. Module 3 introduced nonlinear models and Q-points; the same model-selection and bias ideas reappear here.

Topic 4.1

Device Structure and Physical Operation

Start with the four-terminal structure, then follow the surface from no channel to inversion and pinch-off.

Section introduction

The gate controls charge without direct electrical contact

The defining feature of the MOSFET is the oxide between the gate and semiconductor. The gate behaves like one plate of a capacitor. Its electric field changes the carrier population at the silicon surface, creating a controllable channel while ideally drawing no DC current.

Physical story

  1. At low gate voltage there is no inversion channel.
  2. A positive gate voltage repels holes from the nMOS surface.
  3. At threshold, electrons begin to form a strong inversion layer.
  4. A drain voltage drives current and tapers the channel toward the drain.
  5. At \(V_{DS}=V_{OV}\), the drain end pinches off.

Central definitions

\(V_{OV}\) \(\equiv V_{GS}-V_T\)

\(V_{OV}\) measures how far the gate voltage is above threshold and is the first-order measure of channel strength.

Expanded beginner theory

Build the device from the material layers

The source PDF focuses on an enhancement MOSFET. “Enhancement” means the conducting channel is not present at zero gate bias; gate voltage must create it.

Gate (G)Conductive electrode insulated from silicon by oxide.
Drain (D)Terminal from which conventional nMOS drain current enters.
Source (S)Reference terminal for \(V_{GS}\) and \(V_{DS}\).
Body (B)Semiconductor substrate containing the channel surface.
OxideThin insulating dielectric, commonly represented by \(SiO_2\) in introductory models.
Threshold voltageGate-to-source voltage associated with strong inversion onset.

nMOS enhancement structure

A p-type body contains heavily doped n+ source and drain regions. A positive gate voltage attracts electrons toward the surface and can form an n-type inversion channel.

Why source and drain are initially isolated

Each n+ region forms a pn junction with the p body. Under normal bias, these body junctions are reverse biased, so they do not provide a conducting path through the substrate.

Gate-voltage sequence

Accumulation or weak depletion: at sufficiently low gate voltage, the surface remains hole-rich or only slightly depleted.
Depletion: positive gate charge repels holes, exposing fixed ionized acceptors near the surface.
Inversion: stronger positive gate bias attracts enough electrons that the surface becomes effectively n-type.
Strong inversion: a continuous mobile-electron sheet connects source and drain. Circuit models summarize this onset with \(V_{GS}>V_T\).

Channel charge and overdrive

In a first-order charge-sheet picture, the inversion charge per unit area near the source is approximately proportional to overdrive:

\(Q_n'(0) \approx -C_{ox}V_{OV}\)

The negative sign indicates electron charge. Larger \(V_{OV}\) creates more mobile channel charge and therefore larger conductance.

Small \(V_{DS}\): controlled resistor

The channel charge is nearly uniform. Current is approximately proportional to \(V_{DS}\), and gate voltage controls the effective channel resistance.

Larger \(V_{DS}\): channel taper

The channel potential rises from source to drain. The local overdrive becomes \(V_{GS}-V_T-v(x)\), so charge decreases toward the drain.

Pinch-off and saturation

When \(V_{DS}=V_{OV}\), the inversion charge reaches zero at the drain end. Additional drain voltage drops mainly across the pinch-off region.

What saturation does not mean

It does not mean current becomes zero or carriers stop. It means the first-order current becomes much less sensitive to additional \(V_{DS}\).

Threshold is a model boundary, not a perfect switch

Real MOSFETs conduct subthreshold current below \(V_T\). The source PDF uses the idealized strong-inversion model \(I_D\approx0\) for \(V_{GS}\le V_T\), which is appropriate for first circuit calculations.

Body effect and why source is the voltage reference

If the source and body are not at the same potential, the depletion charge changes and the threshold voltage usually increases for an nMOS with positive \(V_{SB}\). A common supplemental model is

\(V_T=V_{T0}+\gamma\left(\sqrt{2\phi_F+V_{SB}}-\sqrt{2\phi_F}\right).\)

The source PDF does not develop body effect, so the interactive first-order laboratories keep body tied to source unless explicitly noted.

Source Figure 1: MOSFET structure and inversion channel

Concept check before the simulation

Be able to explain why the gate current is nearly zero, why the body junctions are reverse biased, why a positive gate creates an electron channel in nMOS, and why the channel is thinner near the drain when \(V_{DS}>0\).

Interactive laboratory

Channel Formation, Taper, and Pinch-Off

Control \(V_{GS}\), \(V_{DS}\), and \(V_T\) while watching the nMOS surface and current region change.

Laboratory introduction

Translate terminal voltages into local channel charge

The source end sees overdrive \(V_{OV}=V_{GS}-V_T\). Near the drain, the local channel potential is approximately \(V_{DS}\), so the drain-end inversion strength is proportional to \(\max(V_{OV}-V_{DS},0)\).

Recommended sequence

  1. Set \(V_{DS}=0\) and sweep \(V_{GS}\) through threshold.
  2. Hold \(V_{GS}>V_T\) and slowly raise \(V_{DS}\).
  3. Observe channel taper as \(V_{DS}\) approaches \(V_{OV}\).
  4. Enter saturation and identify the pinch-off region.

First-order current model

\(I_D=k_n\left[V_{OV}V_{DS}-\frac{V_{DS}^2}{2}\right]\)
\(I_D=\frac12k_nV_{OV}^2(1+\lambda V_{DS})\)

Cutoff

\(V_{GS}\le V_T\). No strong inversion channel; \(I_D\approx0\).

Triode

\(V_{GS}>V_T\) and \(0\le V_{DS}<V_{OV}\). Channel exists from source to drain.

Saturation

\(V_{GS}>V_T\) and \(V_{DS}\ge V_{OV}\). Drain end is pinched off.

How to interpret the animation

Separate local charge from terminal current

Source-end channel

Its normalized strength is proportional to \(V_{OV}\) when \(V_{OV}>0\).

Drain-end channel

Its normalized strength is proportional to \(\max(V_{OV}-V_{DS},0)\).

Pinch-off

At the boundary, the drain-end channel charge reaches zero, but carriers continue through the high-field pinch-off region.

Channel-length modulation

A nonzero \(\lambda\) models the slight current increase caused by effective channel shortening in saturation.

Topic 4.2

Current-Voltage Models and Region Selection

Use a consistent sign convention, classify the region first, then apply the matching equation.

Section introduction

The source is the reference for both control voltages

For the usual nMOS convention, \(V_{GS}=V_G-V_S\) and \(V_{DS}=V_D-V_S\). Drain current \(I_D\) is defined from drain to source. Region conditions and current equations depend on these signed terminal voltages.

Region decision tree

  1. Compute \(V_{OV}=V_{GS}-V_T\).
  2. If \(V_{OV}\le0\), choose cutoff.
  3. If \(V_{OV}>0\) and \(V_{DS}<V_{OV}\), choose triode.
  4. If \(V_{OV}>0\) and \(V_{DS}\ge V_{OV}\), choose saturation.

Device factor

\(k_n=\mu_n C_{ox}\frac WL\)

Larger mobility, oxide capacitance, or width-to-length ratio increases current for the same terminal voltages.

Extensive beginner derivation

From channel charge to the triode equation

The long-channel model treats the channel as many short differential resistive slices. The local inversion charge decreases as channel voltage rises toward the drain.

Local inversion charge

\(Q_n'(x)=-C_{ox}\left[V_{GS}-V_T-v(x)\right].\)

The local drift current is proportional to mobile charge, mobility, width, and electric field. Integrating from source \(v=0\) to drain \(v=V_{DS}\) gives

\[I_D=\mu_nC_{ox}\frac{W}{L}\int_0^{V_{DS}}\left(V_{OV}-v\right)\,dv\]
\[\boxed{I_D=k_n\left(V_{OV}V_{DS}-\frac{V_{DS}^2}{2}\right)}\]

Why the saturation equation is continuous at the boundary

Substitute \(V_{DS}=V_{OV}\) into the triode equation:

\(I_D=k_n\left(V_{OV}^2-\frac{V_{OV}^2}{2}\right)=\frac12k_nV_{OV}^2.\)

This is exactly the ideal saturation current. The current is continuous even though the equation changes region.

RegionConditionFirst-order currentCircuit interpretation
Cutoff\(V_{GS}\le V_T\)\(I_D\approx0\)Open switch in the ideal strong-inversion model
Triode\(0\le V_{DS}<V_{OV}\)\(k_n(V_{OV}V_{DS}-V_{DS}^2/2)\)Voltage-controlled resistor
Saturation\(V_{DS}\ge V_{OV}\)\(\frac12k_nV_{OV}^2\)Gate-controlled current source
Saturation with CLMSame boundary\(\frac12k_nV_{OV}^2(1+\lambda V_{DS})\)Current source with finite output resistance

Small-\(V_{DS}\) resistance approximation

When \(V_{DS}\ll V_{OV}\), the quadratic term is small:

\[I_D\approx k_nV_{OV}V_{DS}\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad R_{DS}\approx\frac{1}{k_nV_{OV}}\]

A larger gate overdrive produces lower on-resistance.

Worked example A: cutoff

\(V_{GS}=0.8\) V and \(V_T=1.0\) V. Then \(V_{OV}=-0.2\) V, so the ideal strong-inversion model gives \(I_D=0\) for any nonnegative \(V_{DS}\).

Worked example B: triode

Let \(V_{GS}=3\) V, \(V_T=1\) V, \(V_{DS}=0.5\) V, and \(k_n=2\) mA/V². Since \(0.5<2\),

\[I_D=2\left[2(0.5)-\frac{0.5^2}{2}\right]=1.75\ \mathrm{mA}\]

Worked example C: saturation

Keep \(V_{GS}=3\ \mathrm{V}\) and set \(V_{DS}=3\ \mathrm{V}\). Since \(3\ge2\),

\[I_D=\frac12(2)(2)^2=4.00\ \mathrm{mA}\]

Worked example D: CLM

If \(\lambda=0.03\ \mathrm{V^{-1}}\), the previous current becomes

\[I_D=4.00(1+0.03\cdot3)=4.36\ \mathrm{mA}\]

Common region-selection mistakes

  • Comparing \(V_{DS}\) with \(V_{GS}\) instead of \(V_{OV}\).
  • Using saturation merely because \(V_{DS}\) is “large” without checking threshold.
  • Using the saturation equation first and failing to verify \(V_{DS}\ge V_{OV}\).
  • Mixing \(k_n\) definitions that differ by a factor of two. This module uses \(I_{D,sat}=\tfrac12k_nV_{OV}^2\).
  • Mixing A/V² and mA/V².

Interactive laboratory

Output Characteristics: \(I_D\) versus \(V_{DS}\)

Generate a family of curves, inspect the saturation boundary, and evaluate one selected operating point.

Plot-reading introduction

Each curve holds \(V_{GS}\) constant while \(V_{DS}\) changes

Near the origin, current rises approximately linearly. At \(V_{DS}=V_{OV}\), the curve crosses into saturation. With \(\lambda=0\), the ideal saturation portion is physically flat in this model; with \(\lambda>0\), it rises slightly. The graph automatically chooses a y-axis above the largest computed value, so no curve is flattened by display clipping. For a visually and physically continuous boundary, the interactive curves reference channel-length modulation to the onset of saturation: \(I_D=\tfrac12k_nV_{OV}^2[1+\lambda(V_{DS}-V_{OV})]\). The PDF's \((1+\lambda V_{DS})\) form remains shown in the theory section as the common approximate shorthand.

Step-by-step plot interpretation

How to read one operating point

Choose the curve corresponding to the specified \(V_{GS}\).
Compute \(V_{OV}=V_{GS}-V_T\) and mark the boundary at \(V_{DS}=V_{OV}\).
Move horizontally to the specified \(V_{DS}\), then vertically to the selected curve.
Read \(I_D\) and verify that the region condition matches the equation used.
If the saturation curve has slope, estimate \(r_o=(\partial V_{DS}/\partial I_D)_{V_{GS}}\).
